claims.text: Annealing just below the ordering threshold will induce chemical short-range order in an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy.
Annealing-induced chemical short-range order locally enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
The chemically ordered regions create effective domain-wall pinning sites.
Domain-wall pinning produced by chemical short-range order will increase coercivity relative to previously reported soft-ferromagnetic FeCoNi-based derivatives.
The initial alloy is a nearly equiatomic, single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous disordered atomic distribution.
A moderately elevated annealing temperature can provide sufficient atomic mobility for chemical short-range-order formation while remaining below the threshold for decomposition or phase segregation.
Annealing temperature affects ordering, decomposition, and microstructural length scale in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed coercivity enhancement requires retention of a single-phase fcc structure without long-range ordering, precipitation, or phase segregation.
The annealing treatment increases atomic mobility and permits subtle local atomic rearrangements.
Local variations in magnetocrystalline anisotropy caused by chemical short-range order pin magnetic domain walls.
The annealed alloy will have a wider hysteresis loop and a higher coercive field than an as-cast or rapidly quenched FeCoNi-based baseline.
The annealed alloy will maintain high saturation magnetization while its coercivity increases.
As-cast or rapidly quenched FeCoNi-based alloys provide a soft-ferromagnetic, low-coercivity baseline similar to FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
Composition and the length scale of B2 plus BCC decomposition can strongly influence magnetic properties in an Al-Co-Fe-Ni-based high-entropy alloy.
Replacing Co with Cr in AlCoFeNi substantially increases coercivity and reduces saturation magnetization.
Comparing annealed and unannealed batches by structural characterization and magnetometry can test whether chemical short-range order accompanies increased coercivity.
Failure to detect induced chemical short-range order or failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase would falsify the proposed treatment-mediated effect.
